name: Wrenwire Portless AR Wrap Visor
description:
A sleek wraparound AR visor from Wrenwire, a street-label electronics brand operating out of Circuit's eastern fabrication quarter. The frame is matte recycled polycarbonate in deep teal, with a single-piece curved lens that shifts from neutral smoke to near-opaque in high UV. Micro-projectors embedded in the temples cast HUD overlays — navigation, comms, environmental readouts — directly onto the lens surface.

Designed explicitly for users without neural ports, the Portless line relies on gesture-and-blink input. The bridge is padded with antimicrobial silicone and adjustable via a thumb-screw at each temple.
functionality: Delivers AR overlay HUD without BCI requirement. Pairs to personal device via short-range mesh. Photochromic lens adjusts in under 2 seconds. 14-hour battery life; charges via induction strip on inner left temple.
what_it_says: You want the tech but you're keeping your skull your own — practical independence over integration.
worn_by: Tier 2 workers who can't afford BCI but need AR access
manufacturer: Wrenwire (street label, eastern Circuit fab quarter)
story_hooks: Wrenwire's gesture-input firmware has an undocumented passive recording mode — someone is harvesting environmental data from thousands of wearers citywide.
A Tier 3 manager discovers the visor's mesh pairing can tap into unsecured corponation internal feeds if you know the handshake sequence.
The teal colorway was originally a one-off custom run for a now-defunct Circuit collective; wearing original-run teal is a quiet signal in certain circles.
related_entities: Zheng-Dao Bioelectric Galvanic Resuscitation Frame — 'The Pallbearer's Daughter'

physical_description.visual_profile: A sleek, aggressive wraparound visor that dominates the face with a single curved lens extending from temple to temple. The matte teal frame has a futuristic, almost predatory quality—minimal and functional. Sits low on the nose, framing the eyes like a second skin.
physical_description.fit: Snug and adjustable. The silicone bridge pad conforms to the nose, while thumb-screws at each temple allow fine-tuning for different head shapes. Wraps around the face without feeling claustrophobic—designed for extended wear.
physical_description.primary_material: Matte recycled polycarbonate frame (deep teal); curved photochromic composite lens (smoke to opaque); antimicrobial silicone bridge padding
physical_description.texture: Smooth, engineered plastic with a slightly grippy matte finish; lens has a faint iridescent shimmer when light hits it; bridge padding is soft, almost tacky to touch
physical_description.color_scheme: Deep teal matte frame with a neutral smoke-to-clear photochromic lens that darkens under UV. Subtle silver accents around the temple micro-projectors where the frame transitions to lens housings.
physical_description.closures: Thumb-screw adjusters at each temple for size customization; no traditional closure—friction-fit and bridge pressure keep it seated
distinctive_features: Embedded micro-projectors in temple arms for HUD overlay projection
Single-piece curved lens for unobstructed field of view
Gesture-and-blink input sensors (no neural port required)
Minimal Wrenwire circuit-board logo etched on the right temple
Micro-ventilation channels in the frame to prevent lens fogging
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3–4 functional street tech. Too refined for pure salvage (Tier 5), but affordable enough for working-class users. Not corpo-grade (Tier 1–2) precision, but street-made with real engineering.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by people locked out of neural infrastructure—whether by choice, economic circumstance, or ideological resistance. Common among Circuit fabricators, independent contractors, street operators, and augment-skeptics. Signals technical literacy without corpo dependence.
physical_description.condition_typical: Usually worn in and broken-in—the bridge pad shows minor discoloration from skin oils and sweat; the frame may have light micro-scratches; the lens collects dust and fingerprints easily but remains optically clear. Users typically keep it meticulously maintained since it's their primary interface.
